title: 7,000 Restaurants, One Night. How We Rewrote the Rules of Software Deployment
body_markdown:
How disciplined testing, operational rigor, and cross-functional collaboration enabled one of the largest single-night POS deployments in McDonald’s US history.


*by: Sonny Castellano, Manager, Tech Deployment, Mohamed Mahmood, Manager, Tech Deployment & Zainab Tajmahal, Director, Technology Support*


**Quick Byte**


- Scaling restaurant technology isn’t about moving faster; it’s about removing the reasons you have to move slowly
- Years of testing, operational rigor, and continuous improvement turned deployment speed into a byproduct of confidence
- A point-of-sale (POS) update reached 7,000 McDonald’s US restaurants in a single night, proving what’s possible when quality and scale go hand-in-hand


Some nights pass quietly. Others change what a team believes is possible.


During a recent Sesame release, our US Software Deployment Team deployed to **7,000 of 13,500+ US** systemwide **restaurants in a single night.** Half our entire US footprint updated overnight. And this wasn’t just scale for scale’s sake. The U.S. is our largest and most complex market, with diverse restaurant environments and incredibly high operational stakes.


If you’ve never thought about what it takes to run the technology behind a restaurant, here’s the short version: Sesame is McDonald’s point-of-sale (POS) platform that runs all of our restaurant-level transactions across ordering, payment, and operations. That makes it exactly the kind of system teams are careful with. Proving we could update it — safely, at a massive scale, in one night — doesn’t only move Sesame forward; it changes what’s possible for every product built on top of it.


Here’s why we pushed for that scale, and what it actually took to earn it.


**Why deployment speed had to evolve** The restaurant business moves fast. New menu items, new promotions, new ways for guests to order — the pace of change has only accelerated. For a long time, our deployment pace hadn’t kept up. Rolling changes across 13,500+ restaurants used to take weeks, sometimes long enough where one release rollout would still be running when the next one was ready to go.


When our team began rethinking its approach to deployment, we didn’t start by asking, ‘ *how do we deploy faster?’* We asked the better question, *‘How do we remove the reasons we’ve always had to go slow?’*


That reframed the work. Speed was not the goal we chased; it became the outcome we earned by reducing risk, removing uncertainty, strengthening readiness, and building operational confidence at scale.


**The three-year climb to 7,000** None of this happened overnight, and it wasn’t the result of one breakthrough. Prior to 2023, Sesame deployments typically ran **200 to 500 restaurants per night** . Effective at the time — but at that pace, rolling out a single release across 13,500+ US restaurants could take long enough that planning for the next release started before the current one finished.


As the pace of the business accelerated, our US Technology team challenged itself to rethink what was possible. Release after release, teams found ways to streamline processes, strengthen tooling, and build confidence in bigger deployment waves.


**In three years, our minimum deployment velocity grew from 200 to 4,500 restaurants a night — an increase of more than 2,000%.** Peak capacity grew from 500 to 7,000. That’s not an incremental improvement. That’s a fundamentally different way of operating. While reaching all **13** , **5** 00+ US restaurants in a single night remains a future goal, we currently deploy to 7,000 at a time to balance operational risk and minimize potential disruption for crew and customers.


**What it took: Quality first, speed earned** Speed at this scale is only possible if you trust what you’re shipping, and that trust doesn’t happen overnight. It’s the product of a long journey hardening our systems, tightening our testing and security posture, and building a platform where a large-scale push stops feeling like a leap of faith.


For our deployment team, this was never just a deployment target. It was a trust exercise at national scale. A 7,000-restaurant deployment meant thousands of restaurant teams opening their doors the next morning expecting every system to work, every order to flow, and every guest experience to continue without interruption.


The upstream investment had to come first. In partnership with our US Solution Readiness team, we rewrote what ‘ready to deploy’ meant: tighter release criteria, a testing framework built to mirror real restaurant conditions rather than idealized ones, and a hard rule that deployment speed never bought its way past a quality gate. We didn’t reach 7,000 restaurants hoping the release would succeed — our testing gave us evidence, before deployment night, that it would.


A critical part of building that confidence was testing earlier and putting the software into the hands of our Operation Technology Partners (OTP) and other restaurant technology test partners sooner in the development cycle. Their feedback helped strengthen both the stability of the release and the effectiveness of the deployment and installation approach. Across these testing phases, more than 400 individual deployments were successfully executed, giving teams repeated, real-world evidence that the software and installation process were ready to scale. By the time we targeted 7,000 restaurants in a single night, that confidence had been built deployment by deployment.


Just as important was the closed feedback loop. Every prior rollout — large or small — fed directly into how the next one was planned. Restaurant teams, Operations, Field Support, and Development shared one line of sight into emerging issues, so problems got fixed before they became patterns. By the time this deployment was planned, we weren’t estimating risk from scratch. We had a track record to learn from.


**How: The engineering behind the scale** Deploying to 7,000 restaurants in one night meant coordinating upgrades across **100,000+ devices** in a single event.


Three things made that possible:


- **Staged validation, not a single leap.** Controlled readiness testing and stabilization came first, followed by extended observation across a broader restaurant sample, collecting feedback from our restaurant technology test partners, then incremental production waves that validated release quality and operational impact before we ever committed to full scale.
- **Root-cause classification, not a pass/fail bucket.** Incomplete deployments weren’t lumped into one “failure” category — they were classified by cause: software defects, unmet prerequisites, reporting gaps, temporary restaurant conditions, or connectivity issues. That precision meant remediation went exactly where the risk was, instead of everywhere at once.
- **One source of truth, enforced.** Deployment milestones were aligned across teams, restaurant populations were continuously reconciled, and prerequisite readiness was synchronized before dependent features activated. When telemetry and support data disagreed, we reconciled it before it reached a decision-maker. This way, no team was ever making a call off a dashboard that someone else disputed.


We also built a defined exception path — redeployment, investigation, remediation, support follow-up — for any restaurant that didn’t upgrade in the initial window, so stragglers were handled by process, not improvisation.


The result: 7,000 restaurants deployed, minimal operational disruption, and near-zero support impact — one important milestone in Sesame history delivered through close collaboration across McDonald’s Global and Market Technology teams and partners.


> Matt Cava, Director, Solution Readiness, summed up the cross-functional mindset behind the milestone: “As a team, we share a common goal: delivering a restaurant technology platform that is exceptionally stable, reliable, and scalable. Our rigorous testing and deployment practices help ensure that when new releases reach restaurants, operators and crew members experience technology that simply works. Today, we can deploy updates to more than 7,000 restaurants at once, enabling new capabilities to reach a significant share of our US footprint in a single night. This is a testament to the strength of our engineering approach and our continued investment in quality, reliability, and scale.”


**Why this matters beyond one night** The US is our largest and most complex market. The scale, diversity of restaurant environments, and operational stakes are as high as they can get in our System. Proving we could deploy at this speed and scale here isn’t just a win for Sesame, it is a signal to every product team watching, thinking about their own rollout, and a reason for Engineers who want to work on difficult, real-world problems to take a serious look at what we’re building.


This is what modern engineering at McDonald’s actually looks like: distributed systems at a scale most companies never touch, a genuine culture of testing and operational rigor, and a track record of teams that don’t settle for “that’s just how it’s always been done.”


We did more than deploy software to 7,000 restaurants in one night. We proved what speed can look like when it is built on quality, testing, security, and operational discipline.


That’s the part we’re most proud of.
